label: Endogeneity and instrumental variables — mastery test

items.stem: Endogeneity in a simple regression occurs when the regressor is:
items.explanation: Endogeneity means the regressor contains information about the structural disturbance, so the OLS exogeneity condition fails.

items.stem: The standard conditional exogeneity condition is:
items.explanation: Conditional mean zero rules out systematic dependence of the disturbance on the regressors.

items.stem: Instrument relevance for one endogenous regressor requires:
options: a nonzero conditional relationship between Z and X
Z to be uncorrelated with X
items.explanation: The instrument must shift or predict the endogenous regressor after conditioning on included exogenous controls.

items.stem: If Cov(Z,Y)=3 and Cov(Z,X)=1.5, the just-identified IV ratio is:
items.explanation: The IV estimate divides the reduced-form covariance by the first-stage covariance: 3/1.5 = 2. The ratio is measured in outcome units per one-unit change in the endogenous regressor.
items.check: The ratio must exceed 1 because the numerator is twice the denominator.

items.stem: The exclusion restriction requires that the instrument:
options: has no direct effect on Y outside X and is uncorrelated with u
items.explanation: Exclusion rules out a direct instrument-to-outcome path and requires orthogonality to the structural disturbance.

items.stem: A strong first stage is evidence mainly about:
items.explanation: The first stage assesses whether the instrument predicts the endogenous regressor; it cannot prove exclusion.

items.stem: In Y=βX+u, the simple-regression OLS probability limit is:
items.explanation: Substituting Y into Cov(X,Y)/Var(X) gives β+Cov(X,u)/Var(X).

items.stem: If β=2, Cov(X,u)=0.8 and Var(X)=2, the OLS probability limit is:
items.explanation: The OLS probability limit is β plus the covariance term: 2 + 0.8/2 = 2.4. Positive covariance between X and u pushes the slope above the true value.
items.check: The positive covariance adds 0.4 to the true slope.

items.stem: A variable predicts X very strongly but also directly changes Y. It is:
items.explanation: Relevance and exclusion are separate. A direct outcome path violates the exclusion restriction.

items.stem: With a binary instrument, the Wald estimator is:
options: the treatment-rate difference divided by the outcome mean difference
the outcome mean difference divided by the treatment-rate difference
the OLS slope with no controls
the ratio of two standard errors
items.explanation: The reduced-form outcome effect is divided by the first-stage treatment effect.

items.stem: A policy changes mean Y by 0.9 and mean X by 0.3. The Wald IV estimate is:
items.explanation: The reduced-form change 0.9 divided by the first-stage change 0.3 gives 3.

items.stem: Which statement about a weak instrument is correct?
options: It has no first-stage relationship at all
It predicts X only weakly, making IV inference unstable
items.explanation: A weak instrument may satisfy exclusion but provide little predictive variation, leading to imprecise and unreliable IV inference.

items.stem: An overidentification test is available when:
options: there are more excluded instruments than endogenous regressors
there is exactly one instrument for one endogenous regressor
the first stage has zero R²
items.explanation: Overidentifying restrictions arise when the number of excluded instruments exceeds the number of endogenous regressors.

items.stem: Which statements correctly distinguish IV conditions? A. Relevance concerns prediction of X. B. Relevance alone proves exclusion. C. Exclusion rules out a direct Z-to-Y path. D. A strong first stage proves instrument validity.
items.explanation: A and C are true. Relevance concerns the first stage; exclusion concerns the structural path to the outcome. Neither is proved by the other.
statements: Exclusion rules out a direct Z-to-Y path
A strong first stage proves instrument validity

A.why: Statement A is true under the stated IV assumptions.

B.why: Statement B is false because it confuses a separate IV condition or overstates what the data establish.

C.why: Statement C is true under the stated IV assumptions.

D.why: Statement D is false because it confuses a separate IV condition or overstates what the data establish.

items.stem: If Cov(X,u)<0 in the simple regression, the endogeneity term:
options: pushes the OLS probability limit below β
items.explanation: The bias term has the sign of Cov(X,u) because Var(X) is positive.

items.stem: The reduced-form coefficient is 1.2 and the first-stage coefficient is 0.4. The IV estimate is:
items.explanation: The just-identified IV estimate is the reduced-form coefficient divided by the first-stage coefficient: 1.2/0.4 = 3. Multiplying 3 by 0.4 recovers the reduced form.
items.check: Multiply the IV estimate by the first-stage coefficient to recover the reduced form.

items.stem: If Cov(Z,Y)=0.48 and Cov(Z,X)=0.08, the just-identified IV ratio is:
items.explanation: The ratio is 0.48/0.08=6; a small first-stage covariance magnifies the ratio.
items.check: Check 6×0.08=0.48; the denominator is small, so the ratio is large.

items.stem: Consider a proposed instrument. Which statements are valid? A. A first-stage F statistic addresses relevance. B. A large first-stage F proves exclusion. C. A direct Z-to-Y path threatens validity. D. A non-rejection of a J test proves every instrument valid.
items.explanation: A and C are true. First-stage strength is not an exclusion test, and a J-test non-rejection is not proof of validity.
statements: The first-stage F statistic addresses relevance
A large first-stage F proves exclusion
A direct Z-to-Y path threatens validity
A non-rejection of a J test proves every instrument valid

A.why: Statement A is true under the stated IV assumptions.

B.why: Statement B is false because it confuses a separate IV condition or overstates what the data establish.

C.why: Statement C is true under the stated IV assumptions.

D.why: Statement D is false because it confuses a separate IV condition or overstates what the data establish.

items.stem: With heterogeneous treatment effects, a valid binary-instrument Wald ratio may identify:
options: the average effect for every person without assumptions
the effect of Z on Y divided by zero
a local average treatment effect for compliers under additional assumptions
items.explanation: Under independence, exclusion, relevance and monotonicity, the Wald ratio identifies the local average treatment effect for compliers.

items.stem: A reduced-form effect of 0.72 is generated by a first-stage effect of 0.24. The IV estimate is:
items.explanation: The IV ratio is 0.72/0.24 = 3. The instrument-induced outcome change equals 3 times the instrument-induced treatment change.
items.check: The reduced form equals the IV effect times the first-stage effect.
